result.summary: Hesperia, fleeing the amorous Æsacus, is bitten by a snake and dies. In grief Æsacus leaps from a cliff into the sea, and Tethys turns him into a diving bird, the didapper, which keeps trying to drown itself.

scenes.title: The old man identifies the diver
scenes.summary: Observers watching sea birds hear that the didapper was once Æsacus, a Trojan prince, and his lineage is traced from Ilus to Priam.

scenes.title: Hesperia's flight and death
scenes.summary: Æsacus sees Hesperia drying her hair, and she flees. A snake bites her and she dies, and Æsacus blames himself and resolves to die.
scenes.stakes: Hesperia flees for her life, and Æsacus loses his beloved and resolves on death.

place.name: banks of the river Cebrenus, under Ida

scenes.title: Æsacus becomes a didapper
scenes.summary: Æsacus leaps from a cliff, but Tethys turns him into a bird. Resentful, he keeps diving, and his thin form and name come from this.
scenes.stakes: Æsacus is denied the death he seeks and is forced to live on.

alias_notes.explanation: Variant spelling of the nymph's name in the translation.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable image of love wasting Æsacus into the thin-legged bird.

analysis.text: Love and guilt lead to a transformation that perpetuates the lover's grief, like many Ovidian metamorphoses where the form fits the character's passion.
The tale links the Trojan royal house to a natural explanation of a bird's habits and name, in the aetiological tradition of Hellenistic poetry.

fun_facts.text: The Latin name Æsacus is explained by Ovid as coming from the bird's plunging; the translator renders the bird as a didapper, a small diving grebe.

language_notes.text: A didapper is a dabchick or little grebe, a small diving water bird; the name means 'dive-dipper'.
Ilus, Assaracus, Ganymede, Laomedon and Priam are the Trojan royal line. Ganymede was carried off by Jupiter to be his cupbearer.
Hector, Priam's eldest son, was Troy's greatest defender; 'the daughter of Dymas' is Hecuba, mother of Hector.
'Hind' means a female deer; 'water-duck' translates a diving bird, here the hunted prey of the hawk.
Tethys is a sea goddess, wife of Oceanus, so she naturally shelters one who falls into the sea.
The bird's name is explained by its habit of plunging; the etymology is Ovid's own aetiological touch, tied to the Latin/Greek word for diving.

context_notes.text: This summary introduces the tale of Æsacus, one of the many transformations in Book 11 that explain a creature's traits.
Ida is the mountain near Troy; Granicus is a river of the region, and Alexirhoë is his nymph daughter.
Cebrenus was a river god near Troy; his daughters were nymphs, so Hesperie is a river nymph.

literary_notes.text: Hesperia fleeing is compared to a deer escaping a wolf and a duck escaping a hawk, stressing her helpless terror.
Love makes the pursuer swift and fear makes the pursued swift, balancing the two in a neat symmetrical line.
The flight meant to save her life is exactly what ends it; the brief sentence delivers the death abruptly.
The bird's thin body and long neck are explained as lasting marks of lovesick grief.
